newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: China urged to sign Antarctic waters convention.
newsitem.headline: China urged to sign Antarctic waters convention.

text.p: The 21st Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meeting ended in New Zealand on Friday with a call for China to sign an international convention protecting Antarctic waters.
China is building 200 fishing boats aimed at fishing Antarctic and sub-Antarctic waters.
Stuart Prior, head of the New Zealand delegation at the 43-nation meeting, said discussions were being held with China over southern fisheries issues.
"China is not yet a party to the 1980 Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources which governs the Antarctic, although they have signed the Environmental Protocol," he said.
"We understand China is developing a deep water fishery, but it is companies, not their government doing this."
Prior said the Antarctic fishery, particularly the valuable toothfish, was an issue of great concern at the meeting.
High-level moves are under way to stop the illicit plundering of the toothfish by pirate fishing operations.
New Zealand, South Africa, France, Australia and Norway are continuing joint efforts to put an end to the hoovering of the big fish.
The bonanza recently hit a hitch with estimates that there were now 100,000 tonnes of toothfish in storage, and the price has collapsed.
More than 70 vessels are reported to have moved into the new fishery, including ships from treaty nations that switched flags to avoid compliance.
"From the information we have received, pirate fishing in the Southern Ocean is a major problem," Prior said.

"We understand it is being carried out by companies from countries that have signed the protection agreement. But obviously these fishing boats are hiding their origins in order to deceive their governments."
The next treaty meeting will be held in Norway next year.
